coherence.reasons: X's governing thought matches what its evidence supports: seven firm levers reach about 2.6%, and a second wave of about $10M (half of which is needed) closes the gap to 3.0%. The bridge, the lever table, the FY2028 waterfall, the FY2026 covenant path and the one-time budget reconcile with each other. One lapse: slide 11's title says only the margin-first plan 'reaches 3.0%', which holds only with the second wave. Y is cleanly organised by question, and each section sizes its move. But its governing thought ('the margin reaches 3.0% by FY2028') sits above evidence that undercuts it. The 3.02% leaves out the known 2027 wage step, and Y's own backup shows 2.51% with it and 2.96% even after reserves. The headline also counts all nine store exits, while the body defers three of them to a later board vote.

judgment.reasons: Both reject the 8% cut, reprice delivery rather than freeze or close it, prune losing promotions while keeping depth near ValuMart, and stage the store exits. X weighs the trade-offs more carefully. It haircuts the promotion reset by 25% for lost volume and stops at 25% share rather than 24%. It nets $1.5M of reinvested hours against the shrink gain. It puts the wage step and delivery-rate rise in the baseline. It keeps the three vote-dependent stores out of the firm plan, and holds click-and-collect-only as an explicit fallback needing the owners' consent. It also gives a phased FY2026 covenant path (about $25M), a $17M one-time budget against the $25M cap, and a mid-FY2027 trigger. Y's plan is more optimistic: a full 5 pp promotion reset with no lost volume, a shrink gain with no labour cost, all nine exits counted, and the wage rise treated as a risk covered by reserves. One of those reserves is an 8% cut in the best-staffed quartile's hours and the other is shrink back to 2.1%. Y's covenant argument uses run-rate values (3.6 times the need) rather than in-year phasing, and it has no one-time cost budget beyond the $7.5M lease exit.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce the critical numbers correctly: the bridge (e-commerce −0.84 pts, promotions −0.70, shrink −0.50, labour −0.30, about 13%), the −$10.4M e-commerce result, −$12.34 and −$1.64 per order, the fee-test value, and $6.6M / $4.4M for store exits. Both debunk the 6.1% claim and the 'promotions work' correlation. X goes further on several points: it splits the labour change into a wage effect (+1.11 pts) and a productivity effect (−0.77 pts), reconciles the 6.1% step by step, computes break-even incrementality by channel, runs a break-even test on the category team's claim, and gives ranges and sensitivities for every lever. It also labels its own allowances as team estimates. Y matches the answer key's $29.8M gap exactly and its 71% break-even is correct. Its weak point is the shrink clawback: it attributes the whole 0.5 pp shrink rise to hours to get $10.05M, admits this is an upper bound, and then uses it to assert the draft plan lands at $19.8M and misses the covenant. Its promotion and shrink sizings also carry no haircut. X has some unsupported allowances of its own (the vendor-funding sizing, the one-time cost items), but it flags them.

revision.reasons: Both revise management's wage hypothesis on the strength of the bridge: wages are real but explain about 13% of the fall, and productivity absorbed most of the rise. Both replace the across-the-board cut with targeted reallocation and reject the e-commerce freeze as locking in the loss. Both keep what is valid: the wage step remains a headwind, and some targeted labour saving stays in the plan. X is a little more rigorous. It quantifies the shrink clawback as a range ($3.8–7.5M) rather than an upper bound, shows the draft plan's FY2028 outcome (about 1.1%), and tests its own replacement hypothesis, concluding that promotions and delivery alone are not enough. Y's revision is sound, but its claim that the draft plan breaches the covenant rests on the upper-bound shrink estimate.

overall.reasons: Both documents reach a defensible plan of the kind the answer key prefers, with correct diagnosis and the traps avoided. X would serve the CEO better in front of a board and a lender. It is honest that the firm levers reach about 2.6% and says what closes the rest. It builds the known wage and delivery-rate headwinds into the baseline, phases the FY2026 covenant path, budgets one-time cost against the cap, and gives ranges, triggers and a fallback. Y is clear and well sized, but its headline 3.0% depends on leaving out the 2027 wage step, taking no haircut on the promotion reset, and counting three store exits that are not yet approved. Its own appendix shows the plan falling just short once the wage rise is included.
